place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 药园 · 又三年
place.en: Chending Temple · The herb garden · Three more years

setup.zh: 年六那年开春，闵丹师头一回不叫你碾药，把一捆石菖蒲往案上一倒：「你从这一捆里，把能入药的挑出来。」
setup.en: In the spring of the sixth year Pill-master Min, for the first time, does not set you to grinding; he tips a bundle of rock sweet-flag onto the table: "Pick out the ones fit for medicine."

recap.zh: 年六开春，闵丹师教你挑料、教「君」，传你「九节聚气」一方，饭桶照方吐出两纹的丹，八层；「飘风不终朝」，「进退，利武人之贞」，九层；丹房角上一口旁炉，第五炉出一颗一纹的——「我炼的」；第五年腊八你随风、入隙，差一霎赢了大比，观里那颗一转的官丹，揭了封，米汤粘回去，收进了储物袋——转天闵丹师在丹房门口跟你打了个照面，鼻子动了一动；入秋，九层圆满。
recap.en: Year six: Pill-master Min taught you to choose stock and to choose the sovereign, and gave you the Nine-Joint Qi-Gathering recipe; the Rice Tub, fed by it, gave two-ring pills, layer eight; 'a gale does not last a morning', 'it profits a warrior to hold firm', layer nine; a side furnace in the corner of the pill house, one one-ring pill in the fifth batch — "I made it"; at Laba in the fifth year you won the contest by an instant, going with the wind and entering the gap; the temple's one-turn pill, its seal lifted and glued back with rice water, went into the storage pouch — next day Pill-master Min met you at the pill-house door, and his nose twitched; by autumn, layer nine, Consummation.

zh: 「姑娘，五年前你押过他一回。」「输了。」
en: "Miss, five years ago you bet on him once." "Lost."

story.zh:
年六，沈小满十七岁，练气七层。白天他揭执事堂的差事牌，替丹房的闵丹师看炉、碾药；腰里一口暗红的铜剑，叫火柴，脚上一双鯥皮鞋，叫顺风溜——顺风一步十丈。

那年开春，闵丹师头一回不叫他碾药，先考书。那本《金丹》，小满抄过三遍，夜里在柴房里也背，背得比《吐纳经》还熟。闵丹师坐在炉子跟前，眼睛不离炉口，随口道：「『夫金丹之为物』，下一句。」

小满道：「烧之愈久，变化愈妙。黄金入火，百炼不消，埋之，毕天不朽。」

「怎么讲？」

「丹在火里烧得越久，越好。」

闵丹师道：「对了一半。烧得久就好，天底下的丹师都不用学了，架上火，睡一觉便是。」他拿火钳敲了敲炉壁，「要紧的在下一句。《金丹》{典=baopu-jinhuo}说黄金入火，百炼不消——烧得久的前头，先得经得起烧。经不起的，烧一回，是灰；经得起的，烧一回，多一转。丹是这样，料也是这样。」说罢，把一捆石菖蒲往案上一倒，道：「你从这一捆里，把能入药的挑出来。」

小满蹲在案边挑了半天，挑出最粗、最长的七八根，捧过去。闵丹师看也没看，从那一堆里抽出一根细的，细得像一根筷子，拿指甲顺着往下比：「一寸之内，九个节。这一根，抵你那一把。」他把那根菖蒲搁在小满手心里，「草跟人一样，熬过的冬天多，节才密。一年的草，是草；熬过十个冬天、长在石头缝里的，才是药。你看料，先看它熬过几个冬天，再看它长得粗不粗。」

他又从柜里取出一只匣子，里头躺着一截黄精，黑得发亮，比小满见过的都沉：「聚气丹拿黄精做君，人人都会。一炉丹，好坏一半在火，一半在君。君换成年份足的，臣、佐、使跟着换，丹就上一层。」他提笔在一张黄纸上写了四行字，推过来：君，十年黄精；臣，九节菖蒲；佐，茯苓；使，何首乌。「这一方，叫九节聚气。我炼了十年，十炉里出一炉好的。你碾药的时候，心里有数。」说罢，把那截黄精也推了过来，「这一截，算你这个月的碾药钱。」

那天夜里，小满在柴房里，照着那张黄纸，把那截黄精、挑出来的三根九节菖蒲、一把茯苓、一块何首乌，一样一样喂进饭桶。饭桶嚼得极慢，嚼一阵，打一个嗝，嗝里一股菖蒲的清气，熏得小狰直打喷嚏。天快亮的时候，盖子一弹，滚出三颗丹来，颗颗两道纹，比从前的圆，比从前的亮，搁在手心里，沉甸甸地往下坠。他吃了一颗，丹田里那口缸，涨了足足两指。
story.en:
Year six. Shen Xiaoman was seventeen, layer seven of Qi Refining. By day he took tags from the Hall of Errands; by night he kept the furnace and ground herbs for Pill-master Min of the pill house. At his waist hung a dark-red copper sword called the Matchstick; on his feet, a pair of Lu-hide shoes called the Tailwind Slide — with the wind, one step, ten zhang.

That spring, for the first time, Pill-master Min did not set him to grinding; first he tested him on the book. Xiaoman had copied *The Golden Elixir* out three times and recited it at night in the woodshed, until he knew it better than the *Breathing Classic*. Pill-master Min sat by the furnace, eyes never leaving its mouth, and said offhand: "'As for the golden elixir' — the next line."

Xiaoman said: "The longer it burns, the more wondrous its changes. Gold put into fire, refined a hundred times, does not waste; buried, it does not decay till heaven ends."

"Meaning?"

"The longer a pill burns in the fire, the better."

Pill-master Min said: "Half right. If burning long were enough, no pill-master under heaven would need to learn anything — light the fire and go to sleep." He tapped the furnace wall with the tongs. "What matters is the next line. Gold put into fire does not waste — before it can burn long, it has to stand the burning. What can't stand it burns once and is ash; what can burns once and gains a turn. Pills are like that, and so are herbs." With that he tipped a bundle of rock sweet-flag onto the table and said: "Pick out of this bundle the ones fit for medicine."

Xiaoman crouched by the table and picked for a long while, and carried over the seven or eight thickest, longest stems. Pill-master Min didn't look at them. From the heap he drew one thin stem, thin as a chopstick, and ran his fingernail down it: "Nine joints within one inch. This one is worth your whole handful." He laid it in Xiaoman's palm. "A herb is like a man: the more winters it has come through, the closer its joints. A one-year herb is a weed; one that has come through ten winters in a crack of rock — that is medicine. When you look at stock, look first at how many winters it has come through, and only then at how thick it is."

From the cupboard he took a box; in it lay a length of Solomon's seal, black and glossy, heavier than any Xiaoman had held. "Everyone knows to make Solomon's seal the sovereign of the qi-gathering pill. Half of a batch is the fire, half is the sovereign. Change the sovereign for one with years enough in it, change minister, assistant and envoy to match, and the pill goes up a grade." He took a brush and wrote four lines on a sheet of yellow paper and pushed it across: sovereign, ten-year Solomon's seal; minister, nine-joint sweet-flag; assistant, poria; envoy, fleeceflower root. "This recipe is called Nine-Joint Qi-Gathering. I have made it for ten years, and one batch in ten comes out right. Keep it in mind when you grind." With that he pushed the length of Solomon's seal across too. "Call this your grinding wages for the month."

That night in the woodshed Xiaoman followed the yellow sheet and fed the Rice Tub, one thing after another: that length of Solomon's seal, three nine-joint stems of sweet-flag he had picked, a handful of poria, a piece of fleeceflower root. The Tub chewed very slowly; it chewed a while and belched, and the belch smelled clean as sweet-flag and set the little Zheng sneezing. Near dawn the lid sprang open and three pills rolled out, every one of them two-ringed, rounder than any before, brighter, sitting heavy in his palm. He ate one, and the jar in his dantian rose a full two fingers.

label.en: Laba · Up on the stage again

exits.means: year six 闵丹师's lesson in the 丹房 (choosing stock by winters, the 君), the 九节聚气 recipe and a ten-year 黄精; the 饭桶 fed by it gives two-ring pills; 八层; year seven 飘风不终朝 (定风 = waiting it out), 进退 (「初六：进退，利武人之贞」; the pine bough), 九层, the 火柴's line of sparks; a furnace of his own, a true 一纹 pill, 「我炼的」; at Laba in year five he goes up again after four years away, Shopkeeper Qian lists him at one-pays-fifty, A-He's single cash is the only stake; the final against a 九层圆满 won by an instant with 随风 and 入隙, a cut under the ribs; Qian counts out fifty-one cash to her; the sect's one-turn pill resealed with rice water into the storage pouch; 闵丹师's sniff after five years at one furnace; five brides on the Zhang

story.zh:
那年冬天，他过了八层。一口气吸进来，崖顶草屋门口那三根香的烟，都往他这边歪一歪。

每年十月十八，周衡一整天不翻账簿，巡夜的蜡烛也不掰了；每年除夕他去一趟正殿，出来都是那一句「明年，弟子再来」。小满不问。

阿禾那一小条地年年种，年年多半是瘪穗。瞿老只给他定过一条规矩：「差事，你尽管去。蒙山的牌子，不许揭——渡口那个人，知道你是哪里来的。」差事他照揭；每回揭了牌出门，执事堂廊下唱名的那位，总要往簿子上多看一眼。出了山门，后脖颈子上总像落着一双眼睛，回头看，只有风。泗水渡口那个人，五年里再没露过面，像是真在等他找鼎。家信一年两封，他娘的字仍旧又小又密：屋顶不漏了；你爹的膝盖，阴天疼，晴天也疼。内门的单间一间也没空出来，他仍旧睡在西廊那间屋最靠门的那张铺上。大比年年比，头几年，他不上台——他还不到九层，拿了那颗筑基丹也只能揣着，倒招一观的眼睛。

年七，他八层。瞿老那年夏天教的，说是一式，其实是一句话。小满问他：「师父，鯥吸气张翅那一下，为什么一定会来？」瞿老道：「再凶的东西，凶也凶不长。它把一身的劲都使在一声吼、一下撞上，使完了，总得喘一口——你等的，就是那一口。」他念了一句书：「《道德经》{典=laozi-piaofeng}里说：『飘风不终朝，骤雨不终日。』大风刮不了一早上，暴雨下不了一整天。天地使足了劲，都撑不久，何况一头畜生。」他点起一根蜡烛，搁在青石上：「你吹吹看。」小满鼓起腮帮子，使劲吹，火苗子贴着蜡烛倒下去，倒成一条线，可就是不灭；他吹到没气了，火苗子直起来，还是那样。瞿老道：「你吹不灭它。你吹到没气了，它还在。定风，不是站着不动。是等它吹完。」

八层到九层，瞿老教的是进退。那是秋天，他把扫帚把在地上一点，道：「《周易》{典=zhouyi-xun}里，巽卦头一爻，开口两个字：『进退。』整句是：『初六：进退，利武人之贞。』」他拿扫帚把在青石上写了那六个字，「进进退退，是心里拿不定；拿得定的，是武人——一剑出去，全部的灵力，没有退的那一半。」他指着崖边一根碗口粗的松枝：「你砍它。」

小满砍了。一剑下去，剑卡在松枝里，拔不出来——他压进去的是大半口气，留了小半口，怕砍空了收不回来。瞿老道：「你给自己留了一口。」小满拔出剑，又砍，这一回他把丹田里的灵力整个压进剑里，什么也没留，松枝「咔嚓」一声落了地，剑过去，人也过去，收不住，往前冲了两步才站住，缸里一滴灵力也没有了，腿软得像面条。瞿老道：「这才是进退。」他看着崖下，又添了一句，声音低得几乎听不见：「巽四这一宫的剑，不怕慢，不怕软，就怕进退。进了一半想退，那一剑，自己先散了。」顿了一顿，「……剑是这样，别的，也是这样。」

小满那时候没听懂这一句添的是什么。那年腊月之前，他九层了，吸和吐之间，听不出缝来。九层的火柴，一剑出去，剑尖上会甩出一线火星子，细得像灶膛里崩出来的那种——他不知道那是什么，瞿老也没说。

那年秋天，闵丹师在丹房角上那口小炉跟前，给他搁了一只矮凳。那是观里的旁炉，炉壁裂过一道缝，拿泥糊上了；炉底接着丹房那眼地火分出来的一道细缝，火小得像灯芯，一炉只炼三颗。闵丹师只说了一句：「料你自己碾，火你自己看。炼糊了，碾了做药引。」料是丹房的下脚料：碾剩的黄精、黄芪，一捆一捆码在墙角。头一炉，三颗全糊了。第二炉，两颗糊了，一颗没转起来，是一团黑。第五炉，出了一颗，青白，一道纹，歪歪扭扭的，像孩子写的字。他捧着那颗丹去给闵丹师看，闵丹师捏起来，转了一圈，闻了闻，道：「有火气。」又道：「能吃。」这是五年里他从闵丹师嘴里听见的最长的一句夸奖。从此他往阿禾、孙二狗手里塞丹，再不用找由头：丹房里看炉的人，手里有几颗丹，谁也不觉得稀奇；是他炉里炼的，还是饭桶吐的，没人问。

打这以后，丹房角上那口小炉，夜夜亮着一点灯芯大的火。他炼得慢，一个月不过三四炉，炼糊了的照旧碾了做药引。到了腊月，一炉三颗，糊的只剩一颗；开了春，三颗都成了，颗颗一道纹，纹也直了。闵丹师在正炉那头闻了闻，头也不回，道：「火小了。」小满道：「怕糊。」闵丹师道：「怕糊，就一辈子一道纹。首尾武，中间文——你中间那一段文火守得住，头尾那两段武火不敢下。」他走过来，一只手按在炉壁上，灌进去一口灵力，那灯芯大的火「呼」地蹿起半尺，又落了回去。「就这么大。记住这一下。」那一炉，小满头一回炼出了两道纹。到了年八入夏，那口小炉十炉里能出三炉两道纹的；闵丹师正炉开炉，叫他站到炉口跟前看火——这差事，丹房里从前只有闵丹师自己干。丹房的炉是观里的，炼的是手艺；回到柴房，他自己吃的丹，照旧交给饭桶。

那一年腊月，钱掌柜照旧把板子扛上了山，在老槐树底下支开摊子。板上头几行，仍旧是内门的；最底下一行，写的是：**沈小满　一赔五十。**

有人问：「九层了，还一赔五十？」钱掌柜拨着算盘道：「杂灵根拿头名，三百年没出过。」又拨了一下，「四年没上过台。全观记得的沈小满，是四层的、浑身是血、挂在树上的那一个——九层的他出手，谁见过？没见过的，我往大里写。」

阿禾挤到秤盘跟前，放下一文钱。钱掌柜抬起眼皮：「姑娘，五年前你押过他一回。」阿禾道：「输了。」钱掌柜道：「还押？」阿禾道：「他四年没上台，我没处押。」接了纸条，揣好，走了。那一年押沈小满的，统共一文钱。

第五年腊八，刮的是北风。头一场，小满抽着的是内门一个火行的九层。他上了台，头一件事不是看人，是看演武场边上那面旗——旗往南扯。先看风，后看鹿；身后没人替他说，他自己说。他往北边那块青石板上一站，便不挪了。那师兄的火弹一颗接一颗打过来，他拿土墙接，接一颗，碎一面，满台是烟；烟顺着北风，全往南倒，倒进那师兄自己的眼睛里。那师兄咳一声，退半步，咳得眼泪鼻涕一大把，咳到第七声，退到了台边。小满这才走过去，伸手推了一把。掉下台的，输。

中间三场，一场靠脚，一场靠数，一场靠对面那人自己急了，没一场打得好看。决赛的对手，是内门一个九层圆满，等那颗丹等了九年，一上台便是全力，金刃一道接一道。小满躲得开的躲，躲不开的随——随风，剑贴着那金刃往旁边一引，刃上的劲卸去一半，剩下的一半照旧把他往后犁出半尺，脚底下那块厚地稳着；引不开的那几道，他便咬着牙硬挨。半炷香烧到一半，他左边肋下已经开了一道口子，血顺着裤腿流到台上。那师兄的金刃是一口气一口气发的，发一道，喘一口——跟当年的卢方一样。他等的是那一口喘。等到第十一道，那师兄一身的灵力全在刃上，胸前那层光薄了一霎，小满的火柴进去了——不是进人，是进那口喘：剑尖抵在那师兄胸口的衣襟上，停住了。那师兄低头看了看剑尖，看了很久，往后退了一步，退出了台边。掉下台的，输。执事的锣槌在手里转了两转：「沈小满，胜。」

这一回没有猪蜻蜓，也没有镜子，五场，一场一场打下来，打得规规矩矩，台下的人都说没意思。只有小满自己知道，决赛那一剑要是晚一霎，先退出台边的是他。肋下那道口子，缝了七针，长了半个月。周衡把那本蓝布面的名录翻到新的一页，提起笔来，写了「沈小满」三个字，笔停了一停——三百年的名录上，头一回写一个杂灵根的名字。观主把玉盒子放在他手里，封条上盖着大印。

钱掌柜在老槐树底下收摊。阿禾把那张纸条摊在秤盘上，一个字也没说。钱掌柜叹了一口气，解开布袋，一文一文往秤盘上数：「一，二，三……」数得极慢，数一文，嘴角往下耷拉一分。数到二十，围上来七八个人；数到四十，围了一圈，那张胖脸已皱成了一只苦瓜。数到五十，钱掌柜的手在袋口停了一停，又摸出一文，搁在最上头：「本钱。」

阿禾把五十一文拢进帕子里，摸出小本子，翻到五年前那一页。那一页上只一行：**一文。利息另算。**她在底下添了一笔。

钱掌柜把板子往肩上一扛，走出两步，又回过头来，冲小满背上那张弓一抬下巴：「那木头，打听出名字没有？」五年，他年年腊月扛板子上山，见了小满，头一句都是这一句。小满道：「没有。」钱掌柜道：「不急。」

当夜小满在柴房里揭了封条，盒盖一开，一股药气又苦又腥；一道纹，纹边两三点黑斑，一转，下品；饭桶闻了一口，盖上那只小兽拿鼻孔对着他，「噗」地喷出一小股黑烟，炉盖「啪」地一合，再不理他。他讨了半碗米汤，把封条粘了回去，连玉盒子收进储物袋里——全天下唯一一颗他拿出来说得清来历的[筑基丹]{注=foundation-pill}。

第二天他从正殿西北角过，闵丹师正从丹房里出来，两个人打了个照面。五年，隔着一口炉子，一个看火，一个看他。闵丹师的鼻子动了一动——守了三十年炉子的人，鼻子比眼睛灵——目光在他腰上那只储物袋上停了一停。他什么也没说，走了。

这五年，漳水边上，每年十月十八，推下去一只船，船上坐一个穿嫁衣的姑娘。五年，五只船。沉鼎观离漳水十天的路，观里没有一个人知道她们叫什么。周衡知道是哪一天。
story.en:
That winter he passed layer eight.

Every year on the eighteenth of the tenth month Zhou Heng did not open his ledger all day, and did not break his night-watch candle in half; every New Year's Eve he went once to the main hall and came out with the same sentence, "Next year I'll come again." Xiaoman did not ask.

A-He sowed her strip of earth every year, and every year most of the ears were empty. Old Qu gave him one rule, and one only: "Errands, you may go. The Mengshan tags, you don't touch — the man at the ferry knows where you come from." The errands he still took; each time he took a tag and went out, the name-caller in the hall's corridor would look one moment longer at his book. Once outside the gate there always seemed to be a pair of eyes resting on the back of his neck, and when he looked round there was only wind. The man at the Si ferry never showed himself again in five years, as if he really were waiting for him to find the cauldron. Letters came twice a year, his mother's hand still small and dense: the roof doesn't leak now; your father's knee hurts when it's overcast, and when it's clear too. Not one inner-court room of his own came free, and he still slept in the bunk nearest the door of that west-wing room. The contest came round every year; the first few years he didn't go up — he was not yet at layer nine, and had he won that Foundation pill he could only have carried it about, and drawn the whole temple's eyes.

Year seven, layer eight. What Old Qu taught that summer was called a form, but was really one sentence. Xiaoman asked him: "Master, that moment the Lu drew breath and opened its wings — why was it bound to come?" "However fierce a thing is, it can't stay fierce for long," said Old Qu. "It throws all its strength into one roar, one charge, and when that's spent it has to draw breath — that breath is what you wait for." He recited a line: "The *Daodejing* says: 'A gale does not last a morning; a cloudburst does not last a day.' A great wind can't blow a whole morning, a downpour can't fall a whole day. Heaven and earth at full strength can't keep it up — still less a beast." He lit a candle and set it on the bluestone. "Try blowing it out." Xiaoman puffed out his cheeks and blew with all he had; the flame lay flat along the candle, flattened to a line, and would not go out; when he was out of breath it stood up again, just as before. "You can't blow it out," said Old Qu. "When you are out of breath, it's still there. Stilling the wind isn't standing still. It's waiting for the blowing to end."

From layer eight to nine, Old Qu taught Advance-and-retreat. It was autumn. He tapped the broom handle on the ground: "In the *Book of Changes*, the first line of the hexagram Xun opens with two words: 'advance, retreat.' The whole line is: 'First six: advancing and retreating — it profits a warrior to hold firm.'" He wrote the six characters on the bluestone with the handle. "Advancing and retreating is a mind not made up; the one who is made up is the warrior — one stroke out, all the qi, no half kept back for retreating." He pointed at a pine bough at the cliff edge as thick as a bowl's mouth: "Cut it."

Xiaoman cut. The sword stuck in the bough and would not come out — he had put most of a breath into it and kept a little back, afraid of cutting air and not recovering. "You kept a breath back for yourself," said Old Qu. Xiaoman pulled the sword free and cut again, and this time pressed the whole of the qi in his dantian into the blade and kept nothing; the bough came down with a crack, the sword went through and he with it, could not stop, lurched two steps before he stood, not a drop of qi left in the jar, his legs like noodles. "That is advance-and-retreat," said Old Qu. He looked down the cliff and added, so low it could hardly be heard: "The sword of this palace, Xun the fourth, does not fear slow and does not fear soft; it fears advance-and-retreat. Half-way in and wanting to back out, and the stroke falls apart on its own." A pause. "…The sword is like that. Other things, too."

Xiaoman did not understand then what that last sentence had been added for. Before the twelfth month that year he was at layer nine; between the in-breath and the out, no seam could be heard. At nine the Matchstick threw a thin line of sparks off its point with every stroke, fine as what spits out of a stove — he did not know what it was, and Old Qu did not say.

That autumn Pill-master Min set a low stool for him by the small furnace in the corner of the pill house — the temple's side furnace, a crack down its wall daubed over with clay, three pills to a batch. Pill-master Min said only: "Grind your own, watch your own fire. If you burn it, grind it for binder." The herbs were the pill house's leftovers: Solomon's seal and milkvetch ends from the grinding, stacked by the bundle against the wall. The first batch, all three burnt. The second, two burnt and one never turned — a lump of black. The fifth batch gave one pill, pale jade, one ring, lopsided, like a child's writing. He carried it to Pill-master Min, who picked it up, turned it, smelled it, and said: "It has fire in it." And: "It can be eaten." In five years that was the longest praise he heard from Pill-master Min's mouth. After that he could press pills into A-He's and Sun Ergou's hands without hunting for an excuse: a boy who kept the furnace in the pill house having a few pills on him surprised no one; whether he had made them at the furnace or the Rice Tub had spat them out, nobody asked.

From then on, the small furnace in the corner of the pill house showed a fire the size of a lamp-wick every night. He worked slowly, three or four batches a month, and the burnt ones he still ground into guide-powder. By the twelfth month, of three pills only one burned; by spring all three came out, each with one ring, and the rings ran straight. Pill-master Min, over at the main furnace, sniffed without turning his head. "Fire's too small." Xiaoman said: "I'm afraid of burning them." Pill-master Min said: "Afraid of burning, and it's one ring all your life. Strong at both ends, gentle in the middle — you can hold the gentle fire in the middle, but you don't dare give the strong fire at the ends." He came over, laid a hand on the furnace wall and poured in a breath of spirit-power; the wick-sized fire leapt half a foot with a whoosh and fell back. "That big. Remember that." That batch, for the first time, Xiaoman made two rings. By early summer of the eighth year the small furnace gave two-ring pills three batches in ten; when Pill-master Min opened the main furnace he had Xiaoman stand at its mouth and watch the fire — a job no one but Pill-master Min had ever done in that pill house. The pill house's furnace was the temple's, and what he made there was craft; back in the woodshed, the pills he ate himself he still left to the Rice Tub.

That year in the twelfth month Shopkeeper Qian carried his board up the mountain as always and set out his stall under the old locust tree. The first few lines on the board were inner court, as ever; the very last line read: **Shen Xiaoman — one pays fifty.**

Someone asked: "Layer nine now, and still one pays fifty?" Shopkeeper Qian worked his abacus. "A five-door false root taking first — not once in three hundred years." Another flick. "Four years and he's not been up on the platform. The Shen Xiaoman the whole temple remembers is the one at layer four, covered in blood, hanging over a branch like washing — him at layer nine in a fight, who's seen that? What I haven't seen, I write long."

A-He squeezed up to the scale pan and put down one cash. Shopkeeper Qian lifted his eyelids. "Young lady, five years ago you bet on him once." "I lost," said A-He. "Betting again?" said Shopkeeper Qian. "Four years he hasn't gone up," said A-He. "I had nowhere to bet." She took her slip, tucked it away, and left. That year, the whole stake on Shen Xiaoman came to one cash.

At Laba in the fifth year the wind was from the north. In the first bout Xiaoman drew an inner-court fire-root at layer nine. He got up on the platform, and the first thing he looked at was not the man but the flag at the edge of the training ground — it streamed south. Wind first, then the deer; there was no one behind him to say it, so he said it himself. He stepped onto the northern slab and did not budge. The senior's fireballs came one after another; he took them on earth walls, one wall smashed for each ball, till the platform was all smoke; and the smoke went with the north wind, all of it south — into the senior's own eyes. The senior coughed once and gave half a step; coughing up a fistful of tears and snot, and by the seventh cough he had backed to the edge. Only then did Xiaoman walk over and give him one push. Off the platform, you lose.

Three bouts in the middle: one won with his feet, one by counting, one because the man across from him lost his head — not one of them good to watch. His opponent in the final was an inner-court layer nine at Consummation who had waited nine years for that pill, all out from the first step onto the stage, metal blade after metal blade. What Xiaoman could dodge he dodged; what he could not, he went with — Going-with-the-wind, the sword laid along the blade and turning it aside, half its force shed, the other half still ploughing him half a foot backwards, the thick soil under his feet holding; the few he could not turn, he took. By the time the half-stick of incense was half burnt his left side was open under the ribs, blood running down his trouser leg onto the boards. The man's blades came one breath at a time — a blade, then a gasp — the same as Lu Fang had, years ago. It was that gasp he waited for. At the eleventh blade all the man's qi was in the edge, the light over his chest thinned for an instant, and Xiaoman's Matchstick went in — not into the man, into that gasp: the point rested on the front of his robe over the heart, and stopped. The man looked down at the point, looked a long time, and took one step back — off the edge of the stage. Off the stage, and you have lost. The steward's mallet turned twice in his hand: "Shen Xiaoman wins."

This time there was no pig-copter and no mirror: five bouts, fought one after another, all by the book, and the crowd said it was dull. Only Xiaoman knew that had that last stroke come an instant later, it would have been he who stepped off the edge first. The cut under his ribs took seven stitches and half a month.

Shopkeeper Qian was packing up under the old locust tree. A-He spread her slip on the scale pan and said not a word. Shopkeeper Qian sighed, untied his bag, and began counting onto the scale pan one cash at a time: "One, two, three…" — very slowly, the corners of his mouth sagging a notch with every coin. By twenty, seven or eight people had gathered; by forty, there was a ring of them, and his fat face had shriveled into a bitter gourd. At fifty, Shopkeeper Qian's hand stopped at the mouth of the bag; then he took out one more cash and laid it on top. "Your stake."

A-He gathered the fifty-one cash into her handkerchief, took out her little notebook, and turned to the page from five years ago. On it was just the one line: **One cash. Interest charged separately.** Beneath it she added a note.

Shopkeeper Qian swung the board onto his shoulder, went two steps, turned back, and jerked his chin at the bow on Xiaoman's back: "That wood — found out its name yet?" Five years he had carried his board up the mountain every twelfth month, and every year, seeing Xiaoman, that was the first thing he said. "No," said Xiaoman. "No hurry," said Shopkeeper Qian.

That night in the woodshed Xiaoman lifted the seal; the lid opened on a smell both bitter and rank: one ring, two or three dark flecks beside it, one-turn, low grade; the Rice Tub sniffed it once, the little beast on its lid turned its nostrils on him and went "pfft!" — a puff of black smoke — the lid slammed shut, and would have nothing more to do with him. He begged half a bowl of rice water, glued the seal back down, and put it, jade box and all, into the storage pouch — the one Foundation pill in all the world whose history he could tell.

Next day, passing the north-west corner of the main hall, he met Pill-master Min coming out of the pill house. Five years, across one furnace: one watching the fire, one watching him. Pill-master Min's nose twitched — thirty years at a furnace and the nose is sharper than the eyes — and his gaze rested a moment on the storage pouch at Xiaoman's belt. He said nothing, and went on.

In those five years, every eighteenth of the tenth month, a boat was pushed out on the Zhang with a girl in a bridal gown sitting in it. Five years, five boats. Chending Temple was ten days from the Zhang, and no one in it knew their names. Zhou Heng knew which day it was.

exits.means: the autumn month: the lake brims over, layer nine, Consummation; his master calls him up the cliff

refuse.zh: 一季一季来：先过了前头那一季。
refuse.en: One season at a time: finish the one before first.

story.zh:
没过多少日子，丹田里那口水缸满得往外直漾，吸进去一口灵气，便溢出来一口，再也添不进去了——外门的人管这个叫「九层巅峰」；褚先生的名册上，只写四个字：九层圆满。

八月里，瞿老叫他上了一趟崖顶。
story.en:
Before many days had passed, the great jar in his dantian was brimming over: breathe in one breath of spirit and one spilled out; nothing more would go in — the outer court called this "the peak of layer nine"; in Master Chu's register it was written in four characters only: layer nine, Consummation.

In the eighth month, Old Qu called him up to the clifftop.
